claim: High-sugar diet (HSD) feeding leads to decreased body weight in HSD-F0 flies compared to normal diet (ND) flies.
source: Compared to ND flies, HSD-F0 flies exhibited decreased body weight (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing body weight measurements between ND and HSD-F0 flies.

claim: HSD-F0 flies exhibit elevated triglyceride storage levels compared to ND flies.
source: In contrast, their triglyceride and glycogen storage levels, as well as trehalose levels, the major circulating sugar in the fly hemolymph, were elevated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of triglyceride levels shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HSD-F0 flies exhibit elevated glycogen storage levels compared to ND flies.
source: In contrast, their triglyceride and glycogen storage levels, as well as trehalose levels, the major circulating sugar in the fly hemolymph, were elevated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of glycogen levels shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HSD-F0 flies exhibit elevated trehalose levels compared to ND flies.
source: In contrast, their triglyceride and glycogen storage levels, as well as trehalose levels, the major circulating sugar in the fly hemolymph, were elevated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of trehalose levels shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Trehalose is the major circulating sugar in the fly hemolymph.
source: In contrast, their triglyceride and glycogen storage levels, as well as trehalose levels, the major circulating sugar in the fly hemolymph, were elevated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about fly physiology.

claim: The expression levels of DILP2 and DILP5 are downregulated in HSD-F0 flies compared to ND flies.
source: As expected, the expression levels of these genes were downregulated in HSD-F0 flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E measuring mRNA levels of Dilp2 and Dilp5.

claim: DILP2 and DILP5 are released by insulin-producing cells in the fly brain upon nutrient uptake.
source: We therefore quantified the mRNA levels of two important insulin-like molecules in flies, Drosophila insulin-like peptide 2 (DILP2) and DILP5, which were both released by insulin-producing cells in the fly brain upon nutrient uptake (Ikeya et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ikeya et al., 2002.

claim: HSD feeding leads to the development of a diabetes-like phenotype in HSD-F0 flies.
source: These data suggest that HSD feeding leads to the development of a diabetes-like phenotype in the same generation (HSD-F0) as previously reported (Chen et al., 2021; Palanker Musselman et al., 2011; van Dam et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data in the current study and citations to previous reports (Chen et al., 2021; Palanker Musselman et al., 2011; van Dam et al., 2020).

claim: HSD-F1 flies exhibit similar physiological and metabolic changes as HSD-F0 flies despite not experiencing HSD feeding.
source: Furthermore, we also found out that HSD-F1 flies exhibited similar physiological and metabolic changes as HSD-F0 flies despite the former not experiencing HSD feeding (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E), suggesting transgenerational inheritance of metabolic programming upon ancestral HSD exposure (Buescher et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E comparing metabolic parameters between HSD-F1 and HSD-F0 flies.

claim: Ancestral HSD exposure results in transgenerational inheritance of metabolic programming.
source: Furthermore, we also found out that HSD-F1 flies exhibited similar physiological and metabolic changes as HSD-F0 flies despite the former not experiencing HSD feeding (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E), suggesting transgenerational inheritance of metabolic programming upon ancestral HSD exposure (Buescher et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HSD-F1 flies show similar metabolic changes to HSD-F0 flies without direct HSD exposure, and is supported by citation to Buescher et al., 2013.

claim: Insulin signaling plays an important role in feeding regulation.
source: Given that insulin signaling played an important role in feeding regulation (Porte et al., 2002), we first measured total food consumption by the Capillary Feeder (CAFE) assay in HSD-F0 flies (Ja et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Porte et al., 2002.

claim: HSD-F0 flies exhibit significantly increased food consumption compared to ND-fed controls in a 24 hr duration as measured by the CAFE assay.
source: As previously reported, HSD-F0 flies exhibited significantly increased food consumption compared to ND-fed controls in a 24 hr duration (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A); similar increases were observed in HSD-F1 and HSD-F2 flies, too (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the CAFE assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: HSD-F1 and HSD-F2 flies exhibit significantly increased food consumption compared to ND-fed controls in a 24 hr duration as measured by the CAFE assay.
source: As previously reported, HSD-F0 flies exhibited significantly increased food consumption compared to ND-fed controls in a 24 hr duration (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A); similar increases were observed in HSD-F1 and HSD-F2 flies, too (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the CAFE assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: HSD-F0 flies exhibit significantly decreased food consumption compared to ND flies when measured by the MAFE assay during a single meal.
source: However, when we used our previously developed Manual Feeding (MAFE) assay (Qi et al., 2015) to measure the volume of ingested food by individual flies during the course of a single meal, we found that HSD-F0 flies exhibited significantly decreased food consumption (Figure 1D), and that the suppression of meal size was transmitted through multiple generations (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the MAFE assay shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The suppression of meal size in HSD-exposed flies is transmitted through multiple generations.
source: However, when we used our previously developed Manual Feeding (MAFE) assay (Qi et al., 2015) to measure the volume of ingested food by individual flies during the course of a single meal, we found that HSD-F0 flies exhibited significantly decreased food consumption (Figure 1D), and that the suppression of meal size was transmitted through multiple generations (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the MAFE assay shown in Figure 1E demonstrating reduced meal size across multiple generations.

claim: In the MAFE assay, flies are immobilized and presented with microcapillaries filled with liquid food.
source: A major difference between these two feeding assays was that in the MAFE assay flies were immobilized and presented with microcapillaries filled with liquid food, whereas in the CAFE assay flies were free moving and could decide when to feed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used in the study.

claim: In the CAFE assay, flies are free moving and can decide when to feed.
source: A major difference between these two feeding assays was that in the MAFE assay flies were immobilized and presented with microcapillaries filled with liquid food, whereas in the CAFE assay flies were free moving and could decide when to feed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used in the study.

claim: The MAFE assay primarily measures whether flies are responsive to presented food and willing to extend their proboscis to initiate a meal.
source: Therefore, a major determinant of the readout of the MAFE assay was whether flies were responsive to the presented food and were willing to extend their proboscis to initiate a meal, and that of the CAFE assay was flies' overall energy need.
evidence: This is an inference about what the MAFE assay measures based on the experimental design.

claim: The CAFE assay primarily measures flies' overall energy need.
source: Therefore, a major determinant of the readout of the MAFE assay was whether flies were responsive to the presented food and were willing to extend their proboscis to initiate a meal, and that of the CAFE assay was flies' overall energy need.
evidence: This is an inference about what the CAFE assay measures based on the experimental design.

claim: Upon HSD exposure, flies' overall energy expenditure is elevated while their sweet perception is inhibited.
source: Thus, the discrepancy between the results from the CAFE assay and the MAFE assay suggests that upon HSD exposure, flies' overall energy expenditure is elevated while their sweet perception is inhibited, hence their increased food consumption in the CAFE assay but reduced meal size in the MAFE assay.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the contrasting results of the CAFE and MAFE assays.

claim: Both starved and fed HSD-F0 flies show reduced PER responses to various concentrations of sucrose compared to ND-fed controls.
source: We found that both starved and fed HSD-F0 flies showed reduced PER responses to various concentrations of sucrose compared to ND-fed controls (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), and such effect could transmit to following generations till HSD-F4 (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PER assays shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The reduced PER response to sucrose in HSD-exposed flies can transmit to following generations till HSD-F4.
source: We found that both starved and fed HSD-F0 flies showed reduced PER responses to various concentrations of sucrose compared to ND-fed controls (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), and such effect could transmit to following generations till HSD-F4 (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PER assays shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D demonstrating transgenerational effects.

claim: The effect size of acute HSD exposure in HSD-F0 flies is stronger than that in the offspring.
source: It was worth noting that the effect size of acute HSD exposure (in HSD-F0 flies) was stronger than that in the offspring (in HSD-F1 flies and their progeny), which was as expected and with clear biological relevance (Bozler et al., 2019; Klosin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data across generations and citations to Bozler et al., 2019 and Klosin et al., 2017.

claim: Rapid changes in the environment, including alterations in diet, exert immediate and profound impacts on organisms' survival and reproduction, requiring prompt and robust responses.
source: In all living organisms, rapid changes in the environment, including alterations in diet, exert immediate and profound impacts on their survival and reproduction, hence requiring prompt and robust responses.
evidence: This is stated as general biological knowledge.

claim: Clues from ancestral experience may only offer vague and indirect clues of the current living conditions of the offspring.
source: In contrast, clues from ancestral experience may only offer vague and indirect clues of the current living conditions of the offspring.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the nature of transgenerational information transfer.

claim: The body weight and nutrient storage (triglyceride, glycogen, and circulating trehalose) return to normal in HSD-F2 or HSD-F3 flies.
source: For example, the body weight and nutrient storage (triglyceride, glycogen, and circulating trehalose) returned to normal in HSD-F2 or HSD-F3 flies (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), whereas HSD-F2 to HSD-F3 flies still exhibited reduced meal size (Figure 1E) and PER responses to sucrose (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: HSD-F2 to HSD-F3 flies still exhibit reduced meal size despite normalized body weight and nutrient storage.
source: For example, the body weight and nutrient storage (triglyceride, glycogen, and circulating trehalose) returned to normal in HSD-F2 or HSD-F3 flies (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), whereas HSD-F2 to HSD-F3 flies still exhibited reduced meal size (Figure 1E) and PER responses to sucrose (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: HSD-F2 to HSD-F3 flies still exhibit reduced PER responses to sucrose despite normalized body weight and nutrient storage.
source: For example, the body weight and nutrient storage (triglyceride, glycogen, and circulating trehalose) returned to normal in HSD-F2 or HSD-F3 flies (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), whereas HSD-F2 to HSD-F3 flies still exhibited reduced meal size (Figure 1E) and PER responses to sucrose (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: DILP2 and DILP5 expression levels are reduced by HSD exposure from HSD-F0 to HSD-F2 flies but not in HSD-F3 flies.
source: In addition, DILP2 and DILP5 expression levels were both reduced by HSD exposure from HSD-F0 to HSD-F2 flies but not in HSD-F3 flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E; Nässel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E and citation to Nässel et al., 2013.

claim: Altered metabolism or insulin signaling is unlikely to be the causal factor for the reduction in sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior in HSD-exposed flies.
source: Therefore, it was unlikely that altered metabolism or insulin signaling was the causal factor for the reduction in sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior in HSD-exposed flies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that metabolic changes normalize before behavioral changes do.

claim: Both HSD-F0 and HSD-F1 flies exhibit similar gustatory responses to fatty acid (1% hexanoic acid) compared to ND-fed controls.
source: We found that both HSD-F0 and HSD-F1 flies exhibited similar gustatory responses to fatty acid (1% hexanoic acid), another type of appetitive stimuli (Ahn et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2021), compared to ND-fed controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F and citations to Ahn et al., 2017 and Brown et al., 2021.

claim: HSD exposure specifically modulates sweet sensitivity in a transgenerational manner.
source: Therefore, it is likely that HSD exposure specifically modulates sweet sensitivity in a transgenerational manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that HSD affects sweet taste but not fatty acid taste responses.

claim: HSD exposure suppresses sweet sensitivity in male flies, both in HSD-F0 and HSD-F1 flies.
source: But we verified that HSD exposure also suppressed sweet sensitivity in males, both in HSD-F0 and HSD-F1 flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–H.

claim: Transgenerational inheritance can be mediated by the male or female parent.
source: Therefore, transgenerational inheritance could be mediated by the male or female parent as shown in previous work (Daxinger and Whitelaw, 2012; Heard and Martienssen, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Daxinger and Whitelaw, 2012 and Heard and Martienssen, 2014.

claim: The reduction in PER is only seen in F1 flies with HSD-fed female ancestor but not with HSD-fed male ancestor.
source: As shown in Figure 1I, the reduction in PER was only seen in F1 flies with HSD-fed female ancestor but not with HSD-fed male ancestor.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I comparing offspring from HSD-fed female vs. male ancestors.

claim: Only F2 flies with HSD-F1 female ancestor exhibit reduction in PER.
source: Similar results were observed in the F2 generation, that only F2 flies with HSD-F1 female ancestor exhibited reduction in PER (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I.

claim: The effect of HSD exposure is transmitted to offspring via female gametes.
source: These results suggest that the effect of HSD exposure is transmitted to offspring via female gametes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that only female ancestors transmit the behavioral phenotype.

claim: DNA methylation in Drosophila is negligible and limited to the early stages of embryonic development.
source: Despite the importance of DNA methylation in the regulation of vertebrate transgenerational inheritance, it was reported that DNA methylation in Drosophila was negligible and limited to the early stages of embryonic development (Lyko et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lyko et al., 2000.

claim: H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 play important roles in transgenerational inheritance in Drosophila.
source: Multiple lines of research indicated that two types of histone methylations, H3K27me3 and H3K9me3, played important roles in transgenerational inheritance in Drosophila (Coleman and Struhl, 2017; Wang and Moazed, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Coleman and Struhl, 2017 and Wang and Moazed, 2017.

claim: piRNA is associated with altered H3K27me3 and H3K9me3.
source: In addition, piwi-interacting RNA (piRNA), an important species of ncRNA in transgenerational inheritance of Drosophila, was associated with altered H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 (Le Thomas et al., 2014; Peng et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Le Thomas et al., 2014 and Peng et al., 2016.

claim: H3K27me3, H3K27ac, and H3K9me3 are enriched at Hox cluster genes (bxd, Ubx, and Abd-A) as expected.
source: Genomic snapshots of representative target loci (Hox cluster genes: bxd, Ubx, and Abd-A) confirmed H3K27me3, H3K27ac, and H3K9me3 enrichment as expected (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3K27me3 and H3K27ac are widely spread in the genome at mitotic cycle 10-12.
source: Meanwhile, we also observed that H3K27me3 and H3K27ac were widely spread in the genome at this stage, while H3K9me3 was preferentially localized within gene desert regions and heterochromatic regions such as centromeres and pericentromeric (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis, though the data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: H3K9me3 is preferentially localized within gene desert regions and heterochromatic regions such as centromeres and pericentromeric regions at mitotic cycle 10-12.
source: Meanwhile, we also observed that H3K27me3 and H3K27ac were widely spread in the genome at this stage, while H3K9me3 was preferentially localized within gene desert regions and heterochromatic regions such as centromeres and pericentromeric (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis, though the data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: H3K9me2 is nearly undetectable in euchromatic regions during mitotic cycle 10-12.
source: Our analysis also confirmed that H3K9me2 was nearly undetectable in euchromatic regions during this stage (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Upon ancestral HSD exposure, the average peak intensity of H3K27me3 modifications increases significantly.
source: We found that upon ancestral HSD exposure, the average peak intensity of H3K27me3 modifications increased significantly (Figure 2C, upper) whereas the intensity of H3K27ac and H3K9me3 only exhibited modest increase (Figure 2C, middle and lower).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The intensity of H3K27ac and H3K9me3 only exhibits modest increase upon ancestral HSD exposure.
source: We found that upon ancestral HSD exposure, the average peak intensity of H3K27me3 modifications increased significantly (Figure 2C, upper) whereas the intensity of H3K27ac and H3K9me3 only exhibited modest increase (Figure 2C, middle and lower).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Drosophila oocytes transmit repressive H3K27me3 marks to their offspring and exert developmental impact.
source: In addition, previous work has also indicated that Drosophila oocytes transmitted repressive H3K27me3 marks to their offspring and exerted developmental impact (Zenk et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zenk et al., 2017.

claim: Ancestral HSD exposure results in approximately 400 regions with H3K27me3 upregulation distributed throughout the genome.
source: To better understand the upregulation of H3K27me3 peaks in HSD-F1 embryos, we performed differential peaks analysis and found that ancestral HSD exposure resulted in approximately 400 regions with H3K27me3 upregulation (log10 likelihood ratio >3) distributed throughout the genome and 6 H3K27me3 downregulated regions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential peak analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Ancestral HSD exposure results in 6 H3K27me3 downregulated regions.
source: To better understand the upregulation of H3K27me3 peaks in HSD-F1 embryos, we performed differential peaks analysis and found that ancestral HSD exposure resulted in approximately 400 regions with H3K27me3 upregulation (log10 likelihood ratio >3) distributed throughout the genome and 6 H3K27me3 downregulated regions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential peak analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: The signal intensity of H3K27me3 increases remarkably in upregulated regions in HSD-F1 embryos.
source: The signal intensity of H3K27me3 increased remarkably in those upregulated regions (Figure 2D, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The signal intensity of H3K27ac is significantly decreased in H3K27me3 upregulated regions.
source: In these regions, the signal intensity of H3K27ac was significantly decreased (Figure 2D, middle), in line with the antagonism between H3K27ac and H3K27me3 modifications (Tie et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2D and citation to Tie et al., 2009.

claim: H3K27ac and H3K27me3 modifications are antagonistic.
source: In these regions, the signal intensity of H3K27ac was significantly decreased (Figure 2D, middle), in line with the antagonism between H3K27ac and H3K27me3 modifications (Tie et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tie et al., 2009.

claim: H3K9me3 signal remains unchanged in H3K27me3 upregulated regions.
source: Meanwhile, H3K9me3 signal in these regions remained unchanged (Figure 2D, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: H3K27me3 levels in HSD-F1 embryos are significantly increased compared to ND embryos as confirmed by western blot.
source: To validate the ChIP-seq results, we performed western blot on cycle 10–12 embryos and confirmed that the H3K27me3 levels in HSD-F1 embryos were significantly increased compared to ND embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Later-stage HSD-F1 embryos (cycle 13 and 14) exhibit increased H3K27me3 modifications.
source: In line with these results, later-stage HSD-F1 embryos (cycle 13 and 14) also exhibited increased H3K27me3 modifications as directly revealed by H3K27me3 antibody staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: H3K27me3 modifications in the adult stage of HSD-F1 flies are upregulated compared to ND.
source: H3K27me3 modifications in the adult stage of HSD-F1 flies were also upregulated compared to ND (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HSD exposure enhances H3K27me3 modifications in the whole body as well as in the ovary of HSD-F0 flies.
source: We also found that HSD exposure enhanced H3K27me3 modifications in the whole body as well as in the ovary of HSD-F0 flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), further indicating that H3K27me3 modifications are formed in the female germline of HSD-F0 flies and transmitted to the offspring.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: H3K27me3 modifications are formed in the female germline of HSD-F0 flies and transmitted to the offspring.
source: We also found that HSD exposure enhanced H3K27me3 modifications in the whole body as well as in the ovary of HSD-F0 flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), further indicating that H3K27me3 modifications are formed in the female germline of HSD-F0 flies and transmitted to the offspring.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased H3K27me3 in ovaries of HSD-F0 flies.

claim: Polycomb-like protein (Pcl) interacts with Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) to constitute a specific form of PCL-PRC2 complex.
source: Previous studies reported that Polycomb-like protein (Pcl) interacts with Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) to constitute a specific form of PCL-PRC2 complex, which generated high levels of H3K27me3 on specific genomic regions (Nekrasov et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nekrasov et al., 2007.

claim: PCL-PRC2 complex generates high levels of H3K27me3 on specific genomic regions.
source: Previous studies reported that Polycomb-like protein (Pcl) interacts with Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) to constitute a specific form of PCL-PRC2 complex, which generated high levels of H3K27me3 on specific genomic regions (Nekrasov et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nekrasov et al., 2007.

claim: PRC2 complex is comprised of E(z), Su(z)12, Esc, and Caf-1.
source: Besides Pcl, PRC2 complex was comprised of several major components, including enhancer of zeste (E(z)), suppressor of zeste 12 (Su(z)12), extra sex combs (Esc), and chromatin assembly factor-1 (Caf-1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A; Margueron and Reinberg, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Margueron and Reinberg, 2011 and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The mRNA expression of Pcl is upregulated in HSD-F1 and HSD-F2 flies compared to ND controls.
source: By using quantitative RT-PCR, we found that the mRNA expression of Pcl was upregulated in HSD-F1 and HSD-F2 flies compared to ND controls, while mRNA expression of E(z), Su(z)12, Esc, and Caf-1 only exhibited modest yet insignificant changes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: mRNA expression of E(z), Su(z)12, Esc, and Caf-1 only exhibits modest yet insignificant changes in HSD-F1 and HSD-F2 flies.
source: By using quantitative RT-PCR, we found that the mRNA expression of Pcl was upregulated in HSD-F1 and HSD-F2 flies compared to ND controls, while mRNA expression of E(z), Su(z)12, Esc, and Caf-1 only exhibited modest yet insignificant changes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: PCL-PRC2 complex may be involved in the maintenance of H3K27me3 modifications in the offspring upon ancestral HSD exposure.
source: These results suggest that PCL-PRC2 complex may be involved in the maintenance of H3K27me3 modifications in the offspring upon ancestral HSD exposure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of upregulated Pcl expression in offspring.

claim: Pcl and E(z) expressions are not changed in HSD-F0 flies.
source: Paradoxically, Pcl and E(z) expressions were not changed in HSD-F0 flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–G), suggesting that the influence of acute HSD exposure on flies is more complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–G.

claim: Utx and CBP gene expression are downregulated in HSD-F0 flies.
source: For example, we also noted that the Utx histone demethylase (Utx) gene as well as CREB-binding protein (CBP, encoded by nej) gene expression were downregulated in HSD-F0 flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Utx is a H3K27me3 demethylase known to associate with the histone acetyltransferase CBP and to directly block H3K27 trimethylation by E(z).
source: Utx is a H3K27me3 demethylase known to associate with the histone acetyltransferase CBP and to directly block H3K27 trimethylation by E(z) (Tie et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tie et al., 2009.

claim: Knocking down E(z) in nosNGT-GAL4>UAS-E(z) RNAi flies eliminates the transgenerational behavioral deficits.
source: We observed that compared to transgenic controls, nosNGT-GAL4>UAS-E(z) RNAi flies exhibited similar PER responses to sucrose in ND vs. HSD-F1 flies, suggesting the loss of transgenerational behavioral deficits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: nosNGT-GAL4>UAS-E(z) RNAi flies still exhibit reduced PER responses to sucrose in HSD-F0 vs. ND flies.
source: Meanwhile, we observed that nosNGT-GAL4>UAS-E(z) RNAi flies still exhibited reduced PER responses to sucrose in HSD-F0 vs. ND flies, suggesting that E(z) is not required for acute HSD exposure-induced PER reduction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: E(z) is not required for acute HSD exposure-induced PER reduction.
source: Meanwhile, we observed that nosNGT-GAL4>UAS-E(z) RNAi flies still exhibited reduced PER responses to sucrose in HSD-F0 vs. ND flies, suggesting that E(z) is not required for acute HSD exposure-induced PER reduction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that E(z) knockdown doesn't prevent PER reduction in HSD-F0 flies.

claim: Knocking down Pcl generates similar effect as E(z) knockdown on transgenerational behavioral inheritance.
source: Knocking down Pcl, another component of PCL-PRC2 complex, generated similar effect as E(z) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: E(z) and Pcl RNAi treatments do not alter the sweet sensitivity of ND-fed flies across different genotypes.
source: Both E(z) and Pcl RNAi treatments did not alter the sweet sensitivity of ND-fed flies across different genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: RNAi knockdown of Rpd3 and Su(var)3-9 does not affect the transgenerational behavioral inheritance upon ancestral HSD exposure.
source: In contrast, RNAi knockdown of histone deacetylase Rpd3 and H3K9me3 methylase Su(var)3–9 did not affect the transgenerational behavioral inheritance upon ancestral HSD exposure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: H3K27me3 modification plays a crucial role in the transgenerational inheritance of sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior upon ancestral HSD exposure.
source: These data indicate that H3K27me3 modification plays a crucial role in the transgenerational inheritance of sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior upon ancestral HSD exposure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic manipulation experiments showing that disrupting H3K27me3 eliminates transgenerational effects.

claim: Knockdown of E(z) in female germline eliminates H3K27me3 modifications in oocytes and ovary.
source: Knockdown of E(z) in female germline eliminated H3K27me3 modifications in oocytes and ovary, as demonstrated by western blot and immunofluorescence staining (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Knockdown of E(z) and Pcl in female germline eliminates the suppression of PER responses in HSD-F1 flies without interfering with PER responses in ND-fed flies.
source: We found that knockdown of E(z) and Pcl in female germline eliminated the suppression of PER responses in HSD-F1 flies without interfering with PER responses in ND-fed flies (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Knockdown of E(z) and Pcl in female germline does not change PER responses of HSD-F0 toward sucrose.
source: Such treatments but didn't change PER responses of HSD-F0 toward sucrose (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B), either.
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: The transmission of maternal H3K27me3 modifications is critical for the transgenerational inheritance of sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior.
source: These results confirm that the transmission of maternal H3K27me3 modifications is critical for the transgenerational inheritance of sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that maternal germline knockdown of H3K27me3 machinery eliminates transgenerational effects.

claim: EED226 is a potent PRC2 inhibitor that directly binds to the H3K27me3 binding pocket and suppresses H3K27me3 modifications.
source: We tested the effect of EED226, a potent PRC2 inhibitor that directly binds to the H3K27me3 binding pocket and suppresses H3K27me3 modifications (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Loh et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Loh et al., 2021 and western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Feeding EED226 to HSD-F1, HSD-F2 and HSD-F3 flies for five consecutive days restores their PER responses to sucrose to the levels of ND controls.
source: We fed EED226 to HSD-F1, HSD-F2 and HSD-F3 flies for five consecutive days and found their PER responses to sucrose could all be restored to the levels of ND controls (Figure 4A, left and middle).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Chaetocin does not rescue the sweet taste defects in HSD-F1, HSD-F2 and HSD-F3 flies.
source: Chaetocin, a specific inhibitor of H3K9 methyltransferase Su(var)3–9 (He et al., 2012), did not rescue the sweet taste defects in these flies (Figure 4A, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 4A and citation to He et al., 2012.

claim: Feeding HSD-F1 flies with either EED226 or A395 restores sweet responses toward various concentrations of sucrose to the levels of ND-fed controls.
source: We further examined the effect of pharmacological inhibition of H3K27me3 by feeding HSD-F1 flies with either EED226 or A395, another histone methyltransferase inhibitor occupying the H3K27me3 binding sites (He et al., 2017), and found that both treatments restored sweet responses toward various concentrations of sucrose to the levels of ND-fed controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 4B and citation to He et al., 2017.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of H3K27me3 alleviates taste deficits in HSD-F0 flies.
source: Meanwhile, pharmacological inhibition of H3K27me3 alleviated taste deficits in HSD-F0 flies, suggesting that elevated H3K27me3 modifications also partially mediates the effect of acute HSD exposure (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Elevated H3K27me3 modifications partially mediate the effect of acute HSD exposure on taste deficits.
source: Meanwhile, pharmacological inhibition of H3K27me3 alleviated taste deficits in HSD-F0 flies, suggesting that elevated H3K27me3 modifications also partially mediates the effect of acute HSD exposure (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that H3K27me3 inhibition partially rescues taste deficits in HSD-F0 flies.

claim: Feeding EED226 to HSD-F1 flies restores PER responses in both HSD-F1 and their offspring, HSD-F2 flies.
source: To test this, we fed EED226 to HSD-F1 flies and found restored PER responses in both HSD-F1 and their offspring, HSD-F2 flies (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Gustatory neurons expressing Gr5a play a central role in sugar perception.
source: Gustatory neurons expressing a gustatory receptor Gr5a played a central role in sugar perception (Dahanukar et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dahanukar et al., 2007.

claim: Knocking down E(z) in Gr5a+ gustatory neurons restores PER responses in both HSD-F0 and HSD-F1 flies.
source: To directly test this, we knocked down E(z) in Gr5a+ gustatory neurons and indeed found a restoration of PER responses in both HSD-F0 and HSD-F1 flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HSD-F1 flies exhibit significantly reduced calcium transients in Gr5a+ neurons upon sucrose stimulation compared to ND flies.
source: HSD-F1 flies exhibited significantly reduced calcium transients upon sucrose stimulation compared to ND flies, which could be restored by EED226 feeding (Figure 4E, middle and right, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: EED226 feeding restores calcium transients in Gr5a+ neurons of HSD-F1 flies upon sucrose stimulation.
source: HSD-F1 flies exhibited significantly reduced calcium transients upon sucrose stimulation compared to ND flies, which could be restored by EED226 feeding (Figure 4E, middle and right, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The formation of H3K27me3 modifications maintains the silenced state of Drosophila homeobox genes and transmits such a repressive state through multiple rounds of DNA replication in early embryos.
source: Previous work reported that the formation of H3K27me3 modifications maintained the silenced state of Drosophila homeobox genes and transmitted such a repressive state through multiple rounds of DNA replication in early embryos and exerted long-lasting impacts into adulthood (Coleman and Struhl, 2017; Skvortsova et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Coleman and Struhl, 2017 and Skvortsova et al., 2018.

claim: 341 genes correspond to H3K27me3 hypermethylated sites in HSD-F1 flies.
source: To survey a broader range of candidate genes for further analysis, we used less stringent criteria compared to Figure 2 (log10 likelihood ratio >1) and identified ~3000 H3K27me3 hypermethylated regions in HSD-F1 flies using a window of ± 1 kb from the transcription start site and found 341 genes corresponding to hypermethylated sites (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: H3K27me3 often marks the downregulation of gene expression.
source: Since H3K27me3 often marked the downregulation of gene expression, we then asked whether and which of these genes were transcriptionally suppressed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the function of H3K27me3.

claim: RNA-seq analysis identified a total of 133 differentially expressed genes between HSD-F1 and ND flies, including 49 downregulated genes in HSD-F1 flies.
source: To achieve this, we performed RNA-seq analysis using head tissue of HSD-F1 vs. ND flies (Figure 5A) and identified a total of 133 differentially expressed genes (DEG, |log1.5 fold change|>1, p<0.05), including 49 downregulated genes in HSD-F1 flies (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: cad and upd2 are the only two genes located in the H3K27me3 hypermethylated genomic regions and also show downregulated gene expression in HSD-F1 flies.
source: Among these genes, we noticed the homeobox gene caudal (cad), a transcription factor involved in anterior/posterior patterning, organ morphogenesis, and innate immune homeostasis (Mlodzik and Gehring, 1987; Ryu et al., 2008), and unpaired 2 (upd2), a Drosophila leptin ortholog and a secreted factor produced by the fat body which activated JAK/STAT signaling in GABAergic neurons (Hombría et al., 2005; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012), were the only two genes located in the H3K27me3 hypermethylated genomic regions and also showed downregulated gene expression in HSD-F1 flies (Figure 5B–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by integrated analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B–E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: cad is a transcription factor involved in anterior/posterior patterning, organ morphogenesis, and innate immune homeostasis.
source: Among these genes, we noticed the homeobox gene caudal (cad), a transcription factor involved in anterior/posterior patterning, organ morphogenesis, and innate immune homeostasis (Mlodzik and Gehring, 1987; Ryu et al., 2008), and unpaired 2 (upd2), a Drosophila leptin ortholog and a secreted factor produced by the fat body which activated JAK/STAT signaling in GABAergic neurons (Hombría et al., 2005; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012), were the only two genes located in the H3K27me3 hypermethylated genomic regions and also showed downregulated gene expression in HSD-F1 flies (Figure 5B–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mlodzik and Gehring, 1987 and Ryu et al., 2008.

claim: upd2 is a Drosophila leptin ortholog and a secreted factor produced by the fat body which activates JAK/STAT signaling in GABAergic neurons.
source: Among these genes, we noticed the homeobox gene caudal (cad), a transcription factor involved in anterior/posterior patterning, organ morphogenesis, and innate immune homeostasis (Mlodzik and Gehring, 1987; Ryu et al., 2008), and unpaired 2 (upd2), a Drosophila leptin ortholog and a secreted factor produced by the fat body which activated JAK/STAT signaling in GABAergic neurons (Hombría et al., 2005; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012), were the only two genes located in the H3K27me3 hypermethylated genomic regions and also showed downregulated gene expression in HSD-F1 flies (Figure 5B–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hombría et al., 2005 and Rajan and Perrimon, 2012.

claim: Upd2 is mainly expressed in the fat body with clear metabolic functions.
source: Given that Upd2 was mainly expressed in the fat body with clear metabolic functions (Brent and Rajan, 2020; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012), we focused on ubiquitously expressed Cad for further behavioral analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brent and Rajan, 2020 and Rajan and Perrimon, 2012.

claim: HSD-F1 flies exhibit a higher level of H3K27me3 modifications across the genomic region of cad, especially near the promoter region.
source: Notably, HSD-F1 flies exhibited a higher level of H3K27me3 modifications across the genomic region of cad, especially near the promoter region, whereas H3K9me3 signals exhibited no difference (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3K9me3 signals exhibit no difference in the cad genomic region between HSD-F1 and ND flies.
source: Notably, HSD-F1 flies exhibited a higher level of H3K27me3 modifications across the genomic region of cad, especially near the promoter region, whereas H3K9me3 signals exhibited no difference (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cad expression is downregulated in both HSD-F1 and HSD-F2 flies but not in HSD-F0 flies.
source: We also conducted quantitative RT-PCR analysis and confirmed that Cad expression was downregulated in both HSD-F1 and HSD-F2 flies but not in HSD-F0 flies (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Knockdown of E(z) and Pcl in female germline of HSD-F0 flies prevents the decline in Cad expression in HSD-F1 flies.
source: Meanwhile, knockdown of E(z) and Pcl in female germline of HSD-F0 flies prevented the decline in Cad expression in HSD-F1 flies (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Ancestral HSD exposure elevates H3K27me3 levels in the promoter region of cad gene, resulting in a reduction in its mRNA expression in the head tissue of offspring.
source: These data indicate that ancestral HSD exposure elevates H3K27me3 levels in the promoter region of cad gene, resulting in a reduction in its mRNA expression in the head tissue of offspring.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integrated ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing elevated H3K27me3 and reduced cad expression.

claim: Knocking down Cad expression in Gr5a+ neurons leads to lower PER responses to sucrose.
source: Compared to the transgenic controls, knocking down Cad expression in Gr5a+ neurons led to lower PER responses to sucrose (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by PER assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Cad plays an important role in regulating sweet sensitivity in Gr5a+ neurons.
source: These results were consistent with a recent study and confirmed that Cad played an important role in regulating sweet sensitivity in Gr5a+ neurons (Vaziri et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data in the current study and citation to Vaziri et al., 2020.

claim: The reduction in Cad expression likely contributes to the deficits of sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior seen in the offspring of HSD-exposed ancestors.
source: Furthermore, these results suggest that the reduction in Cad expression likely contributes to the deficits of sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior seen in the offspring of HSD-exposed ancestors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Cad knockdown phenocopies the HSD-induced behavioral deficits.

claim: Cad is unlikely to be the only gene that mediates the transgenerational behavioral effect of HSD exposure.
source: It was unlikely that Cad was the only gene that mediated the transgenerational behavioral effect of HSD exposure.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging the complexity of the system.

claim: Ptx1, GATAe, and nub are transcription factors known to regulate sweet sensitivity.
source: Besides Cad, we noticed that several transcription factors, Ptx1, GATAe, nub, which were known to regulate sweet sensitivity (Vaziri et al., 2020), also exhibited elevated H3K27me3 modifications around their promoter regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vaziri et al., 2020.

claim: Ptx1, GATAe, and nub exhibit elevated H3K27me3 modifications around their promoter regions in HSD-F1 flies.
source: Besides Cad, we noticed that several transcription factors, Ptx1, GATAe, nub, which were known to regulate sweet sensitivity (Vaziri et al., 2020), also exhibited elevated H3K27me3 modifications around their promoter regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Ptx1, GATAe, and nub do not show downregulated gene expression in HSD-F1 flies.
source: However, these genes didn't show downregulated gene expression in HSD-F1 flies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Multiple transcriptional regulators may be epigenetically modified by ancestral HSD exposure, which in turn exerts transgenerational effects on the sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior in offspring.
source: It is thus possible that multiple transcriptional regulators are epigenetically modified by ancestral HSD exposure, which in turn exerts transgenerational effects on the sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior in offspring.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential involvement of multiple genes.

claim: Exposure to pathogenic threats in C. elegans induces avoidance memories which can transmit for four generations via sRNA signaling.
source: In C. elegans, exposure to pathogenic threats induces avoidance memories which can transmit for four generations via sRNA signaling (Moore et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Moore et al., 2021.

claim: Exposure to predatory wasps in fruit flies leads to the inheritance of ethanol preference for five generations via maternal NPF repression.
source: In fruit flies, exposure to predatory wasps leads to the inheritance of ethanol preference for five generations via maternal NPF repression (Bozler et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bozler et al., 2019.

claim: Individuals who were exposed to the Dutch Famine in early gestation exhibit deficits in metabolism, cardiovascular health, and mental health.
source: Individuals who were exposed to the Dutch Famine in early gestation exhibited deficits in metabolism, cardiovascular health, and mental health (Schulz, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schulz, 2010.

claim: Mice exposed to traumatic experiences and drugs induce depressive-like or autism-like behaviors in their progeny.
source: Similarly, mice exposed to traumatic experiences and drugs induce depressive-like or autism-like behaviors in their progeny (Chan et al., 2020; Choi et al., 2016; Gapp et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2020, Choi et al., 2016, and Gapp et al., 2014.

claim: HSD is linked to various human diseases, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, and neurobiological diseases.
source: Globally, HSD has become a routine of modern lifestyle, which is linked to various human diseases, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, and neurobiological diseases (Malik and Hu, 2022; Malik et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Malik and Hu, 2022 and Malik et al., 2010.

claim: HSD induces many behavioral disorders in animal models such as feeding abnormalities and addiction-like behaviors.
source: HSD also induces many behavioral disorders in animal models such as feeding abnormalities and addiction-like behaviors (Avena et al., 2009; May et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Avena et al., 2009 and May et al., 2019.

claim: HSD not only affects flies' overall physiology and metabolism within the same generation, but also affects their sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior in a manner spanning multiple generations of offspring.
source: This present study uncovers that HSD not only affects flies' overall physiology and metabolism within the same generation, but also affects their sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior in a manner spanning multiple generations of offspring.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.

claim: Elevated H3K27me3 modifications upon ancestral HSD exposure are the key epigenetic factors underlying the transgenerational regulations of sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior.
source: Mechanistically, our data indicate that elevated H3K27me3 modifications upon ancestral HSD exposure are the key epigenetic factors underlying the transgenerational regulations of sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the mechanistic findings supported by the experimental data throughout the study.

claim: HSD exposure enhances genome-wide H3K27me3 but not H3K27ac or H3K9me2/3 modifications in early embryos.
source: HSD exposure enhances genome-wide H3K27me3 but not H3K27ac or H3K9me2/3 modifications in early embryos.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the ChIP-seq findings.

claim: E(z) and Pcl play a crucial role in catalyzing trimethylation of the repressive chromatin marker histone H3 lysine 27.
source: E(z) and Pcl, the key components of PCL-PRC2 complex, play a crucial role in catalyzing trimethylation of the repressive chromatin marker histone H3 lysine 27, thus maintaining this imprinting during fly development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the function of E(z) and Pcl.

claim: Perturbation of PCL-PRC2 complex blocks the transmission of repressive histone imprinting to offspring and eliminates the transgenerational modulation of sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior.
source: Perturbation of PCL-PRC2 complex, via both genetic and pharmacological approaches, blocks the transmission of such repressive histone imprinting to offspring and eliminates the transgenerational modulation of sweet sensitivity and feeding behavior.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the genetic and pharmacological manipulation experiments.

claim: Epigenetic modulations upon ancestral HSD exposure are transmitted via the female germline.
source: Such epigenetic modulations are transmitted via the female germline, and exert a long-lasting effect on the expression of Cad (and possibly other transcriptional regulators) in the offspring.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings on maternal transmission.

claim: Cad regulates the sensitivity of sweet-sensing gustatory neurons and plays a role in modulating PER responses to sucrose.
source: Cad, a transcription factor belonging to the Hox family, regulates the sensitivity of sweet-sensing gustatory neurons and plays a role in modulating PER responses to sucrose.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings on Cad function.

claim: Feeding behavior is tightly regulated by various factors, such as internal nutritional needs, overall physiological status, and environmental cues.
source: Feeding behavior is tightly regulated by various factors, such as internal nutritional needs, overall physiological status, and environmental cues.
evidence: This is stated as general biological knowledge.

claim: Most regulations of feeding behavior are quite dynamic in nature and do not last for long.
source: However, most of these regulations are quite dynamic in nature and do not last for long.
evidence: This is stated as general biological knowledge.

claim: In fruit flies, energy shortage can trigger foraging and feeding behavior in the timescale of hours, which can be rapidly suppressed upon acquisition of desirable food sources.
source: For example, in fruit flies energy shortage can trigger foraging and feeding behavior in the timescale of hours, which can be rapidly suppressed upon acquisition of desirable food sources (Basiri and Stuber, 2016; Qi et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Basiri and Stuber, 2016 and Qi et al., 2021.

claim: Dynamic regulations of feeding behavior are often mediated by rapid-acting molecular and cellular mechanisms such as ion channels, hormones, and neuropeptides.
source: These regulations are often mediated by rapid-acting molecular and cellular mechanisms such as ion channels, hormones, and neuropeptides (Pool and Scott, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pool and Scott, 2014.

claim: HSD can modulate feeding behavior in a dynamic manner.
source: HSD can also modulate feeding behavior in a dynamic manner (Sung et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sung et al., 2022.

claim: The mechanism of HSD-induced feeding behavior modulation is reversible within the same generation.
source: Moreover, this mechanism is reversible within the same generation.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about HSD effects.

claim: The number of PLCβ2+ taste bud cells in the fungiform papilla decreases within 4 weeks of HSD exposure in mice and is completely restored within 4 weeks upon the removal of HSD.
source: For example, the number of PLCβ2+ taste bud cells in the fungiform papilla decreased within 4 weeks of HSD exposure in mice and was completely restored within 4 weeks upon the removal of HSD (Sung et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sung et al., 2022.

claim: The present study reveals a highly persistent and heritable mechanism of transgenerational modulation of sweet taste perception and feeding behavior that can transmit through multiple generations without re-exposure to the original HSD treatment.
source: However, our present study reveals a highly persistent and heritable mechanism of transgenerational modulation of sweet taste perception and feeding behavior that can transmit through multiple generations without re-exposure to the original HSD treatment.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.

claim: Feeding behavior can be modulated by different regulatory mechanisms with distinct timescales in response to various types of environmental and internal state changes.
source: These findings suggest that feeding behavior can be modulated by different regulatory mechanisms with distinct timescales in response to various types of environmental and internal state changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of dynamic and transgenerational mechanisms.

claim: Some dietary bioactive compounds can regulate histone modifying enzymes.
source: Previous work reported that some dietary bioactive compounds could regulate histone modifying enzymes (Vahid et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vahid et al., 2015.

claim: HSD may directly regulate the activity of histone methyltransferases or histone demethylases.
source: Thus, HSD may directly regulate the activity of histone methyltransferases or histone demethylases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: HSD may affect H3K27me3 modifications via certain nutrient-sensing mechanisms such as O-GlyNAc transferase.
source: Alternatively, HSD may affect H3K27me3 modifications via certain nutrient-sensing mechanisms such as O-GlyNAc transferase, which is known to facilitate H3K27me3 formation with PRC2.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: O-GlyNAc transferase is known to facilitate H3K27me3 formation with PRC2.
source: Alternatively, HSD may affect H3K27me3 modifications via certain nutrient-sensing mechanisms such as O-GlyNAc transferase, which is known to facilitate H3K27me3 formation with PRC2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Long-term memory of H3K27me3 depends on efficient copying of this mark after each DNA replication cycle in a PRC2-dependent manner.
source: Previous work reported that long-term memory of H3K27me3 depends on efficient copying of this mark after each DNA replication cycle in a PRC2-dependent manner (Coleman and Struhl, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Coleman and Struhl, 2017.

claim: PRC2-mediated maintenance of H3K27me3 imprinting can be regulated by dietary exposure.
source: It is therefore possible that PRC2-mediated maintenance of H3K27me3 imprinting can be regulated by dietary exposure.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Cad regulates a network containing 119 candidate genes that are implicated in sensory perception of chemical stimulus, neuropeptide signaling pathways, signal transduction, and transcription factor activity.
source: Previous work has reported that Cad regulates a network containing 119 candidate genes that were implicated in sensory perception of chemical stimulus, neuropeptide signaling pathways, signal transduction, and transcription factor activity, which could impact the sweet gustatory neurons and play a role in modulating PER responses to sucrose (Vaziri et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vaziri et al., 2020.

claim: The Piwi protein negatively regulates H3K27 trimethylation.
source: Especially, as the Piwi protein negatively regulates H3K27 trimethylation (Peng et al., 2016), future studies are needed to understand whether piRNAs, which have been reported to direct transient heterochromatin formation and stabilize maternal mRNAs during embryogenesis (Dufourt et al., 2017; Fabry et al., 2021; Wang and Lin, 2021), are involved in the transgenerational inheritance we identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Peng et al., 2016.

claim: piRNAs have been reported to direct transient heterochromatin formation and stabilize maternal mRNAs during embryogenesis.
source: Especially, as the Piwi protein negatively regulates H3K27 trimethylation (Peng et al., 2016), future studies are needed to understand whether piRNAs, which have been reported to direct transient heterochromatin formation and stabilize maternal mRNAs during embryogenesis (Dufourt et al., 2017; Fabry et al., 2021; Wang and Lin, 2021), are involved in the transgenerational inheritance we identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dufourt et al., 2017, Fabry et al., 2021, and Wang and Lin, 2021.
